correctness.rationale: For an arbitrary order-preserving map, if any occupied target level is represented by a single image point, a pointwise comparable collapse to that point gives a constant in two steps. Otherwise, if one source antichain spans two target levels, choosing its least occupied target level and moving all but one of its least-level images upward produces a comparable map whose least level becomes a singleton, giving a three-edge fence to a constant. If neither situation occurs, each source level maps into one target level and the occupied target levels are strictly increasing. Unequal heights then force an omitted target level when \(h<k\), yielding a one-step pointwise perturbation and the previous singleton case; when \(h>k\), a strictly increasing assignment of \(h+1\) source levels to \(k+1\) target levels is impossible, so one of the earlier cases must occur. The pointwise-comparable-map criterion then converts the fence into finite-space homotopy. The argument uses arbitrary nontrivial antichain sizes and does not extrapolate from finite experiments.

originality.rationale: The modern pseudosphere literature identifies these posets as ordinal sums of trivial posets and studies their order-complex topology, while finite-space homotopy literature supplies the pointwise-comparability criterion for maps. Fresh published-finding search found two genuine partial precedents: unequal-height nullity for binary source levels, and arbitrary height-two source mapping to targets with at least three levels. Neither covers arbitrary finite level sizes at arbitrary unequal source and target heights, especially the \(h>k\) direction. No stronger general theorem implying the audited all-height statement was located.

value.rationale: Weak-order pseudospheres are a natural finite model whose order complexes are joins of discrete sets and hence sphere-like. The theorem gives a complete and unexpectedly rigid cross-height mapping result, including the nontrivial \(h>k\) direction where ordinary sphere homotopy alone would not force nullity. Extending the earlier binary/height-two special cases to arbitrary level cardinalities and all unequal heights is a motivated structural lemma.

final_claim: If \(P=A_0\oplus\cdots\oplus A_h\) and \(Q=B_0\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k\) are finite weak orders with every level of size at least two and \(h\ne k\), then every order-preserving map \(P\to Q\) is finite-space homotopic to a constant map; moreover a constant can be reached through a uniformly short fence of pointwise-comparable maps.
